subject: Using AI for Writing Without Slop: Models, Slides, and BEPs
body:
Hello {firstName},

This week's 🦄 ai that works session was about using AI for writing without turning into a slop factory. Dexter couldn't make it, so Vaibhav was joined by Aaron, co-founder of Boundary, and they walked through how they picked models, how they prepped a conference talk, and how the BAML team writes engineering docs.

The full recording is on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V5X34C9qvX4), and the code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/ai-that-works/ai-that-works/tree/main/2026-11-10-using-ai-for-writing).

**Pick the model for how you like to read, and give it a style guide.** Aaron writes with Opus 5.5 on medium or high. He tried Astra and Sol and found they produce something that reads like a scientific paper. Vaibhav prefers Sol, because he wants facts and bullets, and because speed matters when you can't background the work and go do something else. Both of them tell the model to follow Google's developer documentation style guide, which is public and probably all over the training data. Vaibhav downloaded the whole thing while writing the BAML docs. His rule of thumb: how-to guides can be mostly AI, since people increasingly feed them to agents anyway. Concept pages should stay human.

**Go wide before you go deep.** To prep their talk for a conference in Hamburg, Aaron started with a scratchpad: a title at the top, then a dump of screenshots and half ideas. SpaceX cutting a part's cost from $120,000 to $3,900. How Sentry captures traces. A startup that raised $35 million in 2002 to automate unit testing. No outline yet. Vaibhav's lesson was that if you hand an AI one idea, it follows that one idea. If you seed the context with everything, it can connect pieces you wouldn't have. One result was a real product idea: use profiling to densely trace only the rare arms of a match statement and drop the rest. The human job was knowing when to quit. They couldn't come up with the "going to Mars" equivalent for software, so the Raptor 3 angle got cut, even though the model would happily have invented one.

**Outline before slides, then delete words.** Once the ideas were out, they wrote an outline where every section poses or answers a question from the title. Aaron's test: read just the slide titles in order and see if they tell one simple story. For the slides, Vaibhav tells the AI to delete every word it can, because AI-isms mostly live in sentences, and a slide with five words has nowhere to hide one. He built the deck in plain HTML and JavaScript, abandoned his first worktree when it went sideways, and says Canva and PowerPoint can't touch that iteration speed. He showed an animation where the old tools get swapped out for BAML, and said building that in PowerPoint would need a whole team.

**Make humans the readers, and make the author earn it.** At BAML, design docs are BEPs (BAML enhancement proposals). Authors can use AI freely. Readers can't: the comment system has no API, only a human UI. Authors can reply to comments but can't create them, so the person who produced the doc has more convenience than the person who has to review it. If someone ships slop, they lose BEP privileges and their docs get read last. Authors are expected to flag a rough draft in Slack ("slightly slop, do not read yet"), the way Avery did the night before this session. Aaron also writes every doc as if an entry-level engineer will read it, and frames it as the end-user doc: how will I use this feature, not how is it implemented.

**If you remember one thing from this session:**

Don't spend your energy on whether AI wrote it. Spend it on whether a human cared enough to make it good. Vaibhav's take is that good writing is good writing, the same way good code is good code. Aaron's counterpoint is that readers skim the moment they smell AI. Both are right, which means the thing to do is make someone read every word before it ships. Before you send a doc to a teammate, read it top to bottom yourself and fix the paragraph you'd skip if someone else sent it to you. We don't want teams of Claude talking to Claude.

**Next session: Emergent Behaviors with Gabe Orlanski, creator of SlopCodeBench, tomorrow (November 17th) at 10 AM PT**

Gabe joins us from UW Madison to talk about what's underneath the SlopCodeBench data: new slop patterns appearing or getting worse in models like Fable and Opus 5.5, and how agents do at designing libraries and interfaces. Sign up here: https://luma.com/emergent-slop-behaviors

If you have questions, reply to this email or hop into [Discord](https://boundaryml.com/discord). We read everything.

Happy coding 🧑‍💻

Vaibhav & Dex
